This results in the treasury receiving negligible collateral for massive minting, causing protocol insolvency. The error propagates because all future minting and redemption logic depends on this incorrect conversion, and no other function corrects it.

vulnerabilities.title: protocolMint() Bypasses Collateral Requirement, Enabling Unlimited Free Minting
vulnerabilities.description: The protocolMint() function, callable by AMO_ROLE, mints boost tokens without any collateral transfer. This creates a direct path for attackers with AMO_ROLE to mint unlimited boost tokens at zero cost. Since boost tokens are stablecoins, this dilutes the value of all existing tokens and enables arbitrage attacks where attackers mint tokens and sell them on DEXes for real assets. The economic impact is catastrophic: the protocol’s collateral backing is not increased while supply expands infinitely, leading to depegging and total loss of user confidence. This is a critical access control failure because AMO_ROLE is a privileged role that should be tightly controlled, yet its function has no collateralization check.

vulnerabilities.title: withdrawToken() Allows Unauthorized Withdrawal of Any Token to Treasury
vulnerabilities.description: The withdrawToken() function allows any entity with WITHDRAWER_ROLE to transfer ANY token (including ETH if wrapped, or third-party tokens) from the Minter contract to the treasury. However, the Minter contract may hold tokens deposited by users or received as fees that are not meant to be withdrawn by treasury. This function lacks any validation of token type or balance ownership. An attacker with WITHDRAWER_ROLE can drain all non-collateral tokens held by the contract — including user deposits, reward tokens, or governance tokens — and transfer them to treasury, effectively stealing them. The financial impact is direct theft of any token held by the contract, with no recovery mechanism.

vulnerabilities.title: setTokens() and setTreasury() Lack Reentrancy and State Consistency Protection
vulnerabilities.description: The setTokens() and setTreasury() functions update critical state variables (boostAddress, collateralAddress, treasury) without reentrancy guards or validation of contract state. If these functions are called during an active minting or redemption cycle, they can cause inconsistent state: for example, minting may use old collateralAddress while setTokens() switches it mid-transaction. This creates a race condition where users can mint using the old token address while the new one is being set, leading to collateral being sent to an incorrect or malicious address. The attack requires a front-running transaction or a malicious admin, but the lack of atomicity makes the system vulnerable to state corruption. This is a high-severity data integrity issue because it breaks the fundamental invariant that collateral must be locked in a known, audited address.
vulnerabilities.location: setTokens() and setTreasury() functions, lines 70-78 and 80-83

vulnerabilities.title: Precision Loss in Minting Due to Integer Division Without Validation
vulnerabilities.description: The mint function performs integer division to convert collateral amount to boost amount using (amount / (10 ** (boostDecimals - collateralDecimals))). If boostDecimals < collateralDecimals, this results in a negative exponent, which underflows in Solidity 0.8+ due to unchecked subtraction, causing the division to use an astronomically large denominator, effectively zeroing the transferred collateral. This silently truncates all collateral transfers to zero, allowing attackers to mint unlimited boost tokens without providing any collateral.

vulnerabilities.title: Mathematical Domain Violation: Negative Exponent in Power Operation
vulnerabilities.description: The expression (10 ** (boostDecimals - collateralDecimals)) can compute 10 raised to a negative power when collateralDecimals > boostDecimals. In Solidity, negative exponents in integer exponentiation are undefined and cause underflow (since exponents are uint8). This results in a wraparound to a huge positive number (e.g., 10 ** 250), making the division amount / huge_number == 0. The function does not validate that boostDecimals >= collateralDecimals, violating the mathematical domain requirement that exponents in power operations for currency conversion must be non-negative to avoid loss of precision.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Type System Integrity - Mathematical Domain Validation

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Verification in mint()
vulnerabilities.description: In the mint() function, the collateral transfer (external call) occurs before the mint() call to IBoostStablecoin. If the mint() call reverts (e.g., due to minting cap, paused contract, or invalid recipient), the collateral has already been transferred to treasury. This commits state (funds moved) before verifying the entire operation succeeds, violating operation lifecycle integrity. The caller loses collateral without receiving minted tokens, and treasury gains funds erroneously.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - State Commitment Timing

vulnerabilities.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in protocolMint()
vulnerabilities.description: The protocolMint() function allows AMO_ROLE to mint arbitrary amounts of boost tokens without requiring any collateral or authorization context binding. The function does not validate or bind the amount, recipient, or any external state. An attacker with AMO_ROLE can mint tokens to any address, effectively diluting the entire supply. Since AMO_ROLE is a privileged role that can be granted by ADMIN_ROLE, this is a critical authorization flaw where the operation context (minting without backing) is not constrained by the authorization signature or scope.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Authorization Context Binding

vulnerabilities.title: Interface Definition Incompatibility: IBoostStablecoin.mint() May Require Additional Parameters
vulnerabilities.description: The contract calls IBoostStablecoin(boostAddress).mint(to, amount), assuming a 2-parameter mint function. However, many stablecoin implementations (e.g., MakerDAO’s DAI, Frax’s mint) require additional parameters such as minting fee, sender approval, or reference ID. If the actual IBoostStablecoin contract expects 3+ parameters, the ABI encoding will mismatch, causing the call to revert. This results in mint() failing silently after collateral transfer, leading to funds stuck in treasury with no tokens minted. The interface declaration does not verify compatibility with the actual deployed contract’s function signature.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: External Integration Integrity - Interface Definition Compatibility
